beats.narration_text: Hi — I'm Sudhanva, with this week's STEM explainer for the RL Environments project. IPPO taught our ants to bring food home, including pieces too heavy for one ant. Let's open it up.

props.command: Explain IPPO with our ant colony code: what each ant sees, how it learns, and why two ants end up pulling the same way.
output: grid world · 4 ants · 156 numbers per ant · 6 actions
IPPO after 1M steps: 11.77 of 12 food home · 3 seeds

beats.narration_text: IPPO is plain PPO, with a critic per ant. Each ant decides alone; nothing plans as a team. Yet our ants haul food in pairs. Where does that come from?

props.text:
IPPO is PPO
with one team critic
Each ant decides alone

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the overview is typed line by line, so mid-beat frames are mostly page by design.

beats.narration_text: One ant sees a five-by-five patch of the grid, six layers deep, and six numbers about itself, including which way is home. One shared network, plus an ID tag, turns that into odds over six actions; a separate critic guesses the reward ahead.

beats.narration_text: Then the update. An action that went better than the critic expected gets more likely — but past a twenty percent change from the old policy, the gain is cut off. That clip keeps one lucky rollout from wrecking a working policy.

beats.narration_text: In this code, IPPO and MAPPO differ by one flag. In MAPPO, one critic reads the whole map and scores the team. In IPPO, it scores each ant from its own patch. Both pay each ant half its own reward, plus half the team's average.

shot.new_visual_element: Verbatim code line `centralized_critic: bool = True   # True = MAPPO, False = IPPO`; side by side at the same real state (t=26): MAPPO 517 numbers → one V(s) = 3.23 · IPPO four patches of 156 → V = 3.31 · 3.78 · 3.39 · 3.67; reward line typeset under the verbatim step_r code
shot.visual_intent: SHOW: antrl/algos/ppo.py PPOConfig; run configs differ only in centralized_critic; evidence probe v_mappo / v_ippo; code.state_dim; update() step_r line

beats.narration_text: Crumbs come first; carrying pieces takes off between one and three hundred thousand steps. After a million, IPPO brings home eleven point eight of twelve. The untrained network: zero.

beats.act: the check: why pairs pull together
beats.narration_text: So how do pairs pull together? Holders share a cell, so they see exactly the same thing, and they share weights. Rolling their own dice, untrained ants match one time in ten. Trained, about nine in ten — nearly always toward home. Learned teamwork, riding on shared weights.

shot.new_visual_element: Two holders on one cell; their two 156-number views laid side by side, identical (100% of 3,129 two-holder steps), only the one-hot ID differs; then two paired bars per measure, untrained vs trained, on the same states: same move when each samples 10–12% vs 88–97%; matched pulls heading home 38–40% vs 99%
shot.visual_intent: SHOW: evidence same_view (identical_share, sampled_agree, untrained_sampled_agree, sampled_home_share, untrained_sampled_home_share); greedy agreement 89–99% (week3_v2_results.json transport) shown small
